extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists (students and professionals) writing papers, theses, books, programs, and technical documentation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for clear, correct, and readable mathematical and CS technical writing (papers, theses, program documentation, user manuals). Emphasizes exposition, notation, typography, organization, and editorial process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate symbols in adjacent formulas with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: Consider Sq, q < p. Good: Consider Sq, where q < p. Always place words between adjacent formulas so the reader can parse boundary between expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start a sentence with a symbol; begin with a noun phrase instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: xn − a has n distinct zeroes. Good: The polynomial xn − a has n distinct zeroes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical/compact symbols in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using symbols like ⇒, ∀, ∃, etc., in ordinary exposition; replace them with corresponding words (except in works on logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words such as 'for all', 'there exists', 'implies' in prose. Reserve symbols for displayed mathematics or formal logic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prelude statements before theorems should be complete or end with colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Bad: We now have the following

Theorem. H(x) is continuous.

Good: We can now prove the following result:

Theorem. The function H(x) defined in (5) is continuous.

Prefer also to add motivating wording tying the theorem to prior discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theorem statements self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained, not depending on assumptions only in the preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate necessary definitions or hypotheses within the theorem statement so it can be read independently of nearby paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' to avoid passive but avoid 'I' unless persona matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'we' is useful to avoid passive voice and to create an author–reader dialogue; avoid 'I' in most technical writing unless the author's identity is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' to mean 'you and me together'. For multiple authors, continue to use 'we' or disambiguate ('one author (DEK)', 'the first author') only when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for rhythm and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a definite rhythm in sentences; read your writing aloud and change wording that does not flow smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word choice may vary by context (e.g., 'merge patterns' vs 'merging patterns'); select forms that provide correct cadence and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' when it aids parsing; avoid unnecessary padding
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't omit 'that' when it helps the reader parse the sentence; avoid verbose padding like 'because of the fact that'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Assume that A is a group.' Avoid constructions like 'We have that x = y.' Use judgement and read aloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure; use parallelism where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentence structure and vocabulary to avoid monotony, but use parallelism when parallel concepts are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating unusual words in consecutive sentences. Example (improve parallelism): 'Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid homework-style listing of formulas; provide running commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present a bare sequence of formulas; tie concepts together with explanatory prose and transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why each step matters, provide signposts and motivations rather than just a list of equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State things twice when helpful and define variables on first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to state definitions/important concepts twice, in complementary ways, and define all variables (at least informally) when first introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary restatements reinforce understanding. For long works, restate key definitions before reuse in distant sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate the reader and keep reader knowledge in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Always motivate upcoming results and keep the reader's perspective foremost: what they know, what they expect next, and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing others' work give reasons why it's interesting; when describing your own work be modest and avoid superlatives that distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write so skimming readers can still follow
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers will skim formulas; ensure prose still makes sense if complex formulas are mentally replaced by 'blah'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences should remain coherent without heavy reliance on displayed mathematics; include brief verbal descriptions of formulas' roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation and never reuse a symbol for different meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the same notation for two different things; use the same notation for the same thing across the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain typographic conventions (lowercase for elements, uppercase for sets) and choose index naming to reduce confusion (i from 1..m, j from 1..n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize and manage subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get carried away with subscripts; avoid subscripted subscripts and unnecessary indexing of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer speaking of an element x of X instead of xi when indexing is unnecessary; use set-element notation to avoid proliferation of subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas; number only the important ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Display important formulas on their own line and number only those formulas that are important and will be referenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not number every displayed equation. Give reference numbers to key formulas even if not immediately referenced to aid readers navigating the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sentences readable left-to-right (avoid ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose sentences so they can be parsed left-to-right without ambiguity or garden-path constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Smith remarked in a paper about the scarcity of data.' Better: rewrite to remove ambiguity. Keep modifiers close to the things they modify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out small numbers used as adjectives; not when used as names
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numbers should be spelled out when used as adjectives but left as numerals when used as names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: 'Method 2 is illustrated...' Bad: 'The method requires 2 passes.' Use numerals for counts and names, words for adjectival uses where readability improves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize formal labels (Theorem, Lemma, Algorithm, Method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names like Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Algorithm 3, Method 4 in titles and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent capitalization helps readers spot formal statements; follow the convention throughout the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow core style maxims (prepositions, participles, agreement, punctuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honor standard style maxims: watch sentence-final prepositions, avoid dangling participles, avoid fragments, ensure pronoun antecedent agreement, avoid unnecessary commas, and avoid splitting infinitives unless for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are guidelines rather than absolute rules; use judgement. Some traditional rules can be relaxed for clarity or emphasis but be aware of reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be attentive to spelling and modern hyphenation (nonnegative, nonzero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch common misspellings and note that some compounds like 'nonnegative' and 'nonzero' are no longer hyphenated in current literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spell-checkers and consult field-specific style manuals; maintain consistent spelling across the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' vs 'which' correctly; prefer 'fewer' vs 'less' where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'which' when it is preceded by a comma or preposition or interrogatively; otherwise 'that' usually sounds better. Use 'fewer' for countable quantities and 'less' for uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment to find which sounds better; use commas to mark nonrestrictive clauses that require 'which'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incorrect punctuation before displayed equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place extraneous colons or punctuation before displayed equations if the equation completes the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If C and P are subsets of N^n, let' followed by displayed definition is fine; placing a colon before some displays is wrong. Punctuation around displays should follow conventional logical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a strong opening paragraph and best first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph should be your best paragraph, and its first sentence should be your best sentence to hook readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak opening forms like 'An x is y.' Prefer starting with a meaningful subject and motivation: 'Quicksort is an important method...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow conventional punctuation with quotation marks but be logical with parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas and periods go inside quotation marks by convention; other punctuation stays outside unless part of the quote. Parenthetical punctuation should be logical relative to the contained sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put a period inside parentheses iff the parenthesized content is a complete sentence; otherwise punctuation should be correct if parentheses were removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long noun strings and unnecessary jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist long strings of nouns used as adjectives; avoid using jargon unnecessarily for broader readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: 'packet switched data communication network protocol problem.' Prefer clearer phrasing; use specialist vocabulary only when audience expects it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with humor and exclamation points
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor should be used only when readers clearly understand the technical point behind it; exclamation points should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes must survive rereading; don't overuse excitement punctuation which can distract or annoy technical readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid putting formulas or heavy notation in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use symbols or long formulas in paper titles because they complicate bibliographies and retrieval systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a title needs a technical term, prefer words or short phrases rather than long displayed expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish programming notation from mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-science programming notation (e.g., p[r], * for multiplication) is often inappropriate in formal papers; use mathematical subscript or juxtaposition instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use p_r or p_r (subscript) and xy (no star) in mathematics exposition. Explain when you intentionally use program-like notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise relational nouns (component vs element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific nouns to distinguish relationships (e.g., call p_r a 'component' of p rather than generically an 'element').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear terminology reduces ambiguity between levels of structure (set membership vs component membership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses: place commas and dot-level according to context
rubrics_metrics.description: When using ellipses like (P1, . . . , Pn) put commas before and after the dots; when ellipses are between symbols the dots should be mid-level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with spacing (e.g., '. . .;') and the typographic placement of dots. Use your typesetting system's conventions to avoid odd appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid linebreaks in the middle of formulas and fix spacing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent line breaks inside important formulas; be careful with spaces around ellipses and punctuation inside formulas (TeX has commands to help).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Use TeX features (
obreak, \, \\ and others) to control breaks. Choose correct commands for symbols: use \mid, \emptyset, etc., not imperfection hacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use informative comments and signposts in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short comments like 'We demonstrate the second conclusion by contradiction' or 'There must be a witness...' to inform readers of strategy and progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signposting keeps readers synchronized with goals and subgoals; use headings, paragraph transitions, and explicit strategy statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous parentheses and awkward punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove unnecessary parentheses and extraneous punctuation that distracts; e.g., write 'let k = ci − cj + 1' rather than 'let k be (ci − cj) + 1'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-parenthesized prose and nested parentheses can be tiring. Rework sentence structure to reduce punctuation clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be moderate with typographic devices and fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse typographic tools (many fonts, excessive boldface, many sizes); typographic variety can distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic emphasis sparingly and consistently. For long documents follow design conventions set by book designers or journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a consistent tense strategy (present or sequential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use present tense consistently throughout, or adopt a sequential tense strategy (describe past, present, and future sequentially) for long works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential writing uses phrases like 'We saw this before. We will see this later.' Use words of duration for temporal perspective if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nested delimiters that carry semantic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using brackets or curly braces merely to replace outer parentheses because those symbols have semantic meaning in many fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nested delimiters are unavoidable, typographers use slightly larger outer parentheses; otherwise restructure sentence to avoid nested punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a visible end-of-proof mark and format it clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a box or Q.E.D. at the end of proofs (Halmos box), and leave a space between the box and the final period if used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention signals proof completion. Ensure it doesn't collide with sentence punctuation or create typographic confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraph boundaries clear when using displays
rubrics_metrics.description: When using displayed formulas, take care to show where new paragraphs begin because displays can obscure paragraph breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indentation, extra vertical space, or explicit transitional sentences to mark paragraph starts and ends near displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notational conventions appropriate to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt typographic/notations (boldface, arrows, roman type for 'i+1st' etc.) that your intended audience will understand and expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous forms (e.g., superscript 'st' could be misread); prefer roman type for ordinal suffixes next to math symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'psychologically bad' line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid line breaks that separate a final symbol from its sentence or otherwise create awkward visual parsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonbreaking spaces or tying characters (e.g., tilde in TeX) to keep related tokens together on one line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary indexing by naming elements instead of enumerating
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than giving names to all elements (x1,...,xn) from the outset, use element notation x and y when possible to reduce indexing overhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming only when needed reduces cognitive load; choose indices to reflect roles and stick to them consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols at or before first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Always define symbols before you use them (or at least very near their first use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol is locally defined, place the definition adjacent to the first occurrence; for global symbols, list them early or in a notation section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly monotonous sentence openers; vary transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing successive sentences that start identically ('Thus, ... Consequently, ... Therefore, ...') which produces monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence openers and cadence; use parallelism where the structure is deliberate and aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep index ordering and comparative phrasing consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving relations involving indices, keep the order of indices consistent (e.g., if you say p=(p1,p2,...,pn) and i<j, prefer expressions like pi < pj rather than mixing positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep i and j in same relative positions in statements to avoid reader reorientation and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs to proofs by contradiction for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using proof by contradiction when a clear direct proof is available; direct proofs often make better exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contradiction for discovery or when necessary, but rewrite final exposition as a direct argument when possible to improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material clearly; do not distract the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization is paramount — present material in a way that threads branches and alternatives coherently; avoid distractions that interrupt communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outlines, transitions, and careful structuring of branches and threads. Paul Halmos: 'Do organize' and 'Do not distract.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Signpost goals, strategies, and subgoals in proofs and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what is being proved, the method (case analysis, contradiction, construction), and intermediate aims to keep orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short guiding sentences like 'We will prove...' or 'The proof is in two parts...' improve reader comprehension and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise iteratively; multiple drafts and rewrites improve exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite multiple times; initial handwritten drafts, typed revisions, and later typeset passes reveal different improvements; be willing to scrap and restart if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Knuth's workflow: write in pencil, type and edit for flow, TeX the text, and perform multiple passes. Authors often find different issues at different stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional copy-editing and design for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional copy editors and book designers add value for published books and extensive manuscripts; consider hiring them when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers manage typefaces, margins, chapter headings; copy editors catch punctuation/usage issues and improve consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mathematical typography carefully (font, numerals, slashed fractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select fonts and typographic conventions appropriate to math (e.g., Euler typeface for handwritten look) and distinguish mathematical numerals from text numerals; prefer slashed fractions when they improve readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some fonts change glyph shapes (e.g., zero with dot) and require extra care. Use n(n+1)(2n+1)/3 rather than awkward stacked fractions when it improves readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conservative with gender-neutral pronoun solutions but consider audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices like 'he', 'she', 'his or her', or 'they' have stylistic and audience implications; be mindful of reader expectations and avoid clumsy repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different authorities disagree; choose a consistent approach that suits audience and venue, avoiding constructions that draw attention unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constructions that make readers think about wording too long
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reader must think excessively long about whether a 'which' or comma is correct, the sentence is probably flawed; simplify to reduce reader friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions that parse naturally; when in doubt, restructure the sentence rather than wrestle with punctuation minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distracting usage choices that raise hackles (e.g., controversial 'hopefully')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some word usages (like sentential 'hopefully') provoke strong reactions; if a usage distracts many readers it may be better to avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to minimize stylistic choices that divert attention from content; consult audience expectations and usage panels if necessary.
